title: What Buyers Should Review Before Purchasing a Condominium
content_html:
Buying a condominium is different from buying a single-family home in one important respect: you aren't just buying a unit, you're buying into a legal and financial relationship with an association that governs the building, the grounds, and your obligations as an owner. California law gives condo buyers a bundle of documents meant to make that relationship visible before you're locked into the purchase. Knowing what's in that bundle — and what to actually look for in each piece — is one of the most useful things a buyer can do during a condo transaction.

Why Condo Documents Matter More Than They Seem To

A single-family home's condition is largely about the structure itself and what a home inspector can find. A condo's condition is also about the health of the association that maintains the roof, the exterior walls, the common landscaping, the pool, and often the plumbing risers and shared systems you'll never personally see or control. An association with healthy reserves, clear governing rules, and no pending litigation is a very different ownership experience than one that's underfunded, in disrepair, or embroiled in a lawsuit — even if the units themselves look identical. The documents are how you find out which situation you're actually buying into.

The CC&Rs: The Rulebook for the Property

The Declaration of Covenants, Conditions and Restrictions — almost always just called the CC&Rs — is the foundational legal document for the community. It defines what's common area versus what's part of your individually-owned unit, what architectural changes you can and can't make, rental restrictions, pet policies, and the association's authority to levy assessments and enforce rules. If you plan to rent the unit out, run a home-based business, or make modifications down the road, the CC&Rs are where you find out whether that's allowed before you own the property, not after.

Bylaws and Operating Rules

Bylaws govern how the association itself operates — board elections, meeting procedures, voting rights, and officer duties. Operating rules (sometimes called rules and regulations) are typically more specific day-to-day policies: parking assignments, pool hours, noise rules, and similar details. Board elections and member voting rights for most California common interest developments are governed by the Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act.[1] A buyer curious about how much say they'll actually have in how the community is run can get a fuller picture of how that process works in a separate guide to HOA board elections and voting rights.

The Budget and Reserve Study

This is where the financial health of the association becomes visible. The current operating budget shows what the association collects and spends in a typical year. The reserve study — a periodic analysis of the association's major shared components (roofs, paving, pool equipment, and similar big-ticket items) and how much money is set aside to replace them when they wear out — is arguably the single most important document in the entire package for a prospective buyer. An association that is significantly underfunded relative to its reserve study's recommendations is an association that will likely need to levy a special assessment at some point to cover the gap, and that bill lands on whoever owns the unit at the time.

Meeting Minutes

Board meeting minutes, usually for the past year or so, are one of the most underused documents in a condo purchase. This is where disputes, planned repairs, litigation discussions, insurance issues, and rule changes actually show up in writing before they become a line item on a budget or a special assessment notice. A buyer who only reads the CC&Rs and skips the minutes can miss a brewing issue that the board already knows about but hasn't yet had to formally disclose elsewhere.

Financial Statements and Delinquency Rates

Look at the association's financial statements for signs of financial stress: a pattern of deficit spending, a high rate of homeowner delinquency on dues, or litigation reserves being tapped for operating expenses. A high delinquency rate among unit owners doesn't just signal individual financial trouble — it directly affects how much money the association has on hand to maintain the property and respond to emergencies, and it can also affect whether the unit qualifies for certain types of financing.

Insurance Coverage

Condo associations typically carry a master insurance policy covering the building structure and common areas, while the unit owner is responsible for a separate HO-6 policy covering the interior of their own unit, personal property, and liability. Understanding where the master policy's coverage ends and your own policy needs to begin is important — ask for a copy of the master policy's declarations page and, if anything is unclear, have your own insurance agent review it before closing.

Pending Litigation and Assessments

Associations are generally required to disclose pending or anticipated litigation involving the common areas. Construction defect litigation, disputes with contractors, or disagreements with individual owners can all affect both your ownership experience and your ability to sell or refinance later. Related to this, find out whether any special assessments have been levied recently or are under discussion — these are one-time charges beyond regular dues, often tied to a major repair or a reserve shortfall, and buyers are sometimes surprised to learn one is pending only after they've already opened escrow.

How This Connects to the Broader Disclosure Process

Condo-specific documents are one part of a larger disclosure picture in a California home purchase. Sellers still owe buyers the general disclosures that apply to any residential transaction, and it's worth understanding how those two tracks — general seller disclosures and condo/HOA-specific documents — fit together. For a broader view of what a seller is required to disclose generally, see this overview of California seller disclosure requirements, and for an explanation of the recurring dues themselves, this guide to understanding HOA fees before you buy covers how monthly assessments are typically structured.

A Practical Review Checklist

  • CC&Rs — ownership boundaries, use restrictions, rental and pet policies
  • Bylaws and operating rules — governance and day-to-day policies
  • Current budget and most recent reserve study
  • Board meeting minutes, generally the past year
  • Financial statements and delinquency information
  • Master insurance policy declarations page
  • Any pending or anticipated litigation
  • Recent or upcoming special assessments

Give Yourself Time to Actually Read Them

These documents often arrive as a thick packet late in the process, which tempts buyers to skim or skip them entirely. That's a mistake. If something in the CC&Rs, the reserve study, or the minutes raises a question, it's worth asking before contingencies are removed, not after. A real estate attorney or your agent can help flag the sections that matter most for your specific situation, particularly if you're planning to rent the unit, make modifications, or if the reserve study shows a funding level that concerns you.
